---
title: "Reports for Management Decisions"
---


::: {.learning-objectives}
## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Design a report page for a named reader and decision, with key performance indicators shown against their comparisons and a layout that passes a five-second test.
2. Build drill-through pages and report-page tooltips that let a reader move from a summary to its detail.
3. Model a budget at the grain of month, account, and cost center beside the ledger, and explain a budget variance as volume, classification, timing, rate, or spending.
4. Write visual calculations for running sums and moving averages, and decide when a measure in the model is the better choice.
5. Assemble a reporting package with navigation, an About page, and validation.
6. Use what-if parameters and the Analytics pane's forecast, and judge their results against the models of Chapter 7 and the Part II case.
:::


## Opening Scenario {.unnumbered}

It is April 2027, and the controller wants Charles River Reports to become the company's monthly reporting package. "Three people will open it first," she says. The sales manager wants to know what the promotions of fiscal 2026 cost and which ones cost the most. The department managers want to see how their spending compared with the budget the CFO approved. The production manager wants to know whether the plant's hours are under control, the question Part III answered with queries. A first look at the budget already shows why the package needs care: one department spent far less than its budget and another far more, and neither result means what it seems to mean.

Your task is to design a page for each of these readers, to connect the pages so that a reader can move from a summary to the rows behind it, and to make sure each number is explained before it reaches someone who will act on it. This chapter teaches the design of report pages, drill-through and tooltip pages, budget-versus-actual reporting, visual calculations, and the assembly of a documented package, and it closes with two tools that look ahead: what-if parameters and forecasts.


## Designing Reports for Their Readers

A report page serves a reader who has a question and a decision to make. The pages of Chapters 13 and 14 were built for exploration by the person who built them. The pages of this chapter are built for readers who did not build the model, may not know DAX, and will give the page a few seconds before deciding whether it answers their question. Design therefore starts with the reader: what decision the page supports, what the reader must compare to make it, how much detail the reader needs, and how often the page will be read.

A key performance indicator (KPI) is a measure chosen because it tracks progress toward an objective, shown with the comparison that gives it meaning. A number on its own says little. Operating expense of several million dollars is neither good nor bad until the reader knows the budget, the same period last year, or a target. Few (2013) argues that a display meant for monitoring should fit on one screen and show each measure in the context that lets the reader judge it at a glance. Few calls such displays dashboards. Power BI, as Chapter 13 explained, reserves that word for a page of tiles in the Power BI service, so this chapter says report page.

Research on performance reports shows that the choice and the presentation of measures shape the judgments readers make. Lipe and Salterio (2000) found that superiors evaluating two business units relied on the measures common to both units and ignored the measures unique to each. A package that compares department managers should therefore give every department the same KPIs, defined the same way. Cardinaels and van Veen-Dirks (2010) found that adding markers for above-target, below-target, and on-target performance changed how heavily evaluators weighted the measures. Formatting is not neutral. A marker should appear only where it signals something the reader should act on, and its threshold should be stated.

The layout follows the reader's path. The KPI and its comparison go at the top left, where the eye starts. The breakdown that explains it comes next, and the detail behind it is available on demand, through the drill-through pages and tooltips of the next section, rather than crowding the page. A useful check is a five-second test: show the page to someone for five seconds and ask what it says. If they cannot answer the question the page exists to answer, the page needs a simpler design. @tbl-15-01 lists the readers of the Charles River package and what each page must show, and @fig-15-01 maps the package.

| Reader | Question | KPI and its comparison | Page |
|------------|----------------------|----------------------|----------|
| Sales manager | What did the promotions cost, and where? | Revenue from list price to net, by step; discounts by promotion | Promotions |
| Department manager | Is my cost center within its budget? | Operating expense against the budget, flexed for volume | Budget |
| Production manager | Are the plant's hours under control? | Hours per standard hour over twelve months | Plant |
| Controller | Do the pages agree with the ledger? | Control totals of earlier chapters | Validation |

## Drill-Through and Report-Page Tooltips

Chapter 6 defined drill-down as moving from a total to the parts or rows behind it, and the matrix of Chapter 13 drills down by expanding an item group into its product types. Drill-down stays inside one visual. Drill-through moves the reader to another page, filtered to the item the reader selected. On a page that lists the promotions, the reader right-clicks one promotion and chooses **Drillthrough**, and Power BI opens a detail page that shows only that promotion: its terms, its discounts month by month, and its invoice lines. The detail page holds the drill-through field in a well of its own, and Power BI adds a back button to it automatically. The field must also appear in the visual the reader right-clicks, or the option does not appear (Microsoft, 2026d). This is how a report lets managers explore causes on their own, as Chapter 1 promised, without placing every detail on the summary page.

A report-page tooltip is a small report page that appears when the reader points at a data point, filtered to that data point. It replaces the default tooltip, which only repeats the values of the visual, with a chart or a few numbers chosen for the purpose. A tooltip page is set to the tooltip canvas size and switched on as a tooltip in its page settings, and a visual can be told which tooltip page to use. Tooltips are for quick context. They are not interactive, and screen readers cannot read them, so nothing the reader must know should appear only in a tooltip (Microsoft, 2026c). @tbl-15-02 compares the three ways of moving from a summary to detail, and @fig-15-02 contrasts drill-down with drill-through.

| | Drill-down | Drill-through | Report-page tooltip |
|------------|-------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| What changes | The level shown in the same visual | The page, filtered to the selected item | A small page shown while pointing |
| How the reader starts it | Expand a level or use the drill buttons | Right-click, then Drillthrough | Point at a data point |
| Best for | Moving down a hierarchy | Studying one item in detail | A quick second view |
| Accessible to screen readers | Yes | Yes | No |

: Three ways to move from a summary to detail {#tbl-15-02}

![Drill-Down Within a Visual and Drill-Through to Another Page.](/visuals/svg/fig-15-02-drill-down-through.svg){#fig-15-02 fig-alt="Two panels. On the left, drill-down: a matrix row for Furniture expands into its product types inside the same visual. On the right, drill-through: a bar for one promotion on the Promotions page is right-clicked, the Drillthrough menu offers Promotion Detail, and an arrow leads to a separate page filtered to that promotion, with a back button in its corner."}

## Budget Versus Actual

A budget is a plan expressed in the accounts of the ledger, and comparing it with the ledger is the most common management report there is. Charles River's budget, which Chapter 7 analyzed in a workbook, is a second fact table. Each line of BudgetLine is one account, one month, and one cost center, with the item on the sales and cost-of-sales lines, and each year's lines were approved by the CFO in the December before. To compare the budget with the ledger, the two fact tables must share dimensions: Account, CostCenter, and Date. Account and CostCenter relate to BudgetLine on their keys, exactly as they relate to GLEntry. Date needs care, because a budget line has a month but no day. Microsoft's guidance for facts recorded at a higher grain than the date table is to store the first day of each period and relate that date to the date table (Microsoft, 2025c). The budget then adds up correctly by month, quarter, and year, but a visual that shows days would place each month's budget on its first day, so budget measures are read by month or above.

A budget variance is the difference between an actual amount and its budget. This book computes it as actual less budget, so for an expense a positive variance means spending above the budget, which is unfavorable, and a negative variance is favorable; for revenue the signs mean the opposite. Variance percent divides the variance by the budget. A report must say which convention it uses, because a reader who assumes the other will reach the wrong conclusion.

A variance measures a difference. It does not explain one. @tbl-15-03 lists the usual causes, and Charles River's 2026 operating expense shows four of them at once. The Sales department spent far less than its budget, but most of the difference is volume: the commission budget was calculated on the budget's sales volume, which Chapter 7 found to be several times the actual, so the commission flexed to actual sales, Chapter 7's flexible budget applied to one variable cost, is much smaller. The Warehouse spent more than its budget and Administration less, and the two differences offset: depreciation was budgeted entirely in Administration but recorded partly in the Warehouse. Chapter 2 warned that a budget-versus-actual report misleads when the budget and the ledger classify the same cost differently, and this is that case. Once volume and classification are set aside, almost every cost center is a few percent under budget, which is the payroll burden rate that Chapter 7 found budgeted well above the actual rate. And the months with three pay dates, which Chapters 11 and 14 traced, are unfavorable against a budget that spreads salaries evenly, while the other months are favorable.

| Cause | What happened | Charles River, fiscal 2026 |
|------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| Volume | Activity differed from the budget's assumption | Commission budgeted on the budget's sales volume |
| Classification | The budget and the ledger record the cost in different places | Depreciation budgeted in Administration, recorded partly in the Warehouse |
| Timing | The cost fell in a different month from the budget | Salaries paid in months with three pay dates |
| Rate | The price per unit differed from the budget's | Payroll burden below the budgeted rate |
| Spending | More or less was used than planned | What remains after the other causes |

: Causes of a budget variance {#tbl-15-03}

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
Charles River's sales budget plans several times the volume the company actually sold, so revenue and cost of goods sold fall far short of their static budget every month. A page that compares them with the static budget shows enormous unfavorable revenue variances and favorable cost variances that say nothing about how the year went. Flex the budget to actual volume first, as Chapter 7 did, or leave revenue off the page and say why.
:::

The page should signal the variances that need attention without relying on color alone, the rule that Chapters 4 and 6 set and Chapter 13 applied to every visual. Power BI's conditional formatting can place an icon beside a value according to rules, such as an arrow pointing up for spending more than five percent above budget, a circle for spending within five percent, and an arrow pointing down for spending more than five percent below. An icon whose shape differs, with the signed percentage beside it, carries the meaning in grayscale and to a reader who does not see color (Microsoft, 2025a).


## Visual Calculations

A visual calculation is a DAX calculation defined on a single visual, which works on the rows and columns that the visual already shows (Microsoft, 2026f). It is stored with the visual, not in the model. Because it works on the visual's own rows, a running sum, a moving average, or a comparison with the previous row takes one short formula. You add one by selecting a visual and choosing New visual calculation on the Home tab, which opens an editor showing the visual, a formula bar, and the visual's rows as a grid, called the visual matrix. Templates write the common calculations for you (Microsoft, 2026a).

Visual calculations have functions of their own. RUNNINGSUM adds each row to the rows before it, MOVINGAVERAGE averages a number of rows ending at the current one, PREVIOUS returns the value of the row before, and FIRST the value of the first row. An optional argument names the direction in which the calculation moves through the visual, down the rows or across the columns, and another restarts it at each change of a higher level, such as each year in a visual of months. They are the visual's counterparts of the window functions of Chapter 11, as @tbl-15-04 shows: the order of the rows in the visual plays the part of ORDER BY, restarting at a higher level plays the part of PARTITION BY, and the number of rows in a moving average plays the part of the frame.

| Visual calculation | What it returns | SQL counterpart (Chapter 11) |
|-----------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| `RUNNINGSUM` | The running total down the rows | `SUM` with an `OVER` clause ending at the current row |
| `MOVINGAVERAGE` | The average of the last n rows | `AVG` over a frame of n rows |
| `PREVIOUS` | The value of the previous row | `LAG` |
| `FIRST` | The value of the first row | `FIRST_VALUE` |
| `COLLAPSE` | The value at the parent level | A window partitioned by the parent |

: Visual calculation functions and their SQL counterparts {#tbl-15-04}

The same property that makes visual calculations simple limits them. A visual calculation sees only the rows of its visual. If a chart of trailing twelve-month ratios is filtered to start in January 2025, the moving average for January 2025 has one month to average, not twelve, because the eleven months before it are not on the visual. A measure written with the time intelligence of Chapter 14 reaches into the model and finds them. Visual calculations also cannot be reused in another visual, are left out when a reader exports the data, and cannot be pinned to a dashboard (Microsoft, 2026f). The rule of thumb follows: a calculation that shapes how one visual reads, such as a year-to-date line on one chart, can be a visual calculation; a number that readers rely on, compare across pages, or export belongs in the model as a measure, with a description and a test. @tbl-15-05 compares the three places a calculation can live, and @fig-15-06 shows the editor with a calculation from Tutorial 15.2.

| | Measure | Visual calculation | Calculated column |
|------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Defined in | The model | One visual | A table of the model |
| Sees | The whole model, through the filter context | Only the rows and columns of its visual | The current row and related rows |
| Calculated | When a visual asks for it | When its visual is drawn | At refresh, and stored |
| Reused elsewhere | Yes | No | Yes |
| Exported with the data | Yes | No | Yes |

: Where a calculation can live {#tbl-15-05}

![The Visual Calculation Editor.](/visuals/svg/fig-15-06-visual-calc-editor.svg){#fig-15-06 fig-alt="A mock of Power BI's visual calculation editor. At the top, a preview of a table visual of months with the variance against the flexed budget. Below it, the formula bar holds the visual calculation YTD Variance equals RUNNINGSUM of Variance to Flexed. At the bottom, the visual matrix lists each month of fiscal 2026 with its variance and the running total, which rises in January, falls through June, rises again in July, and ends the year favorable. A Back to report button sits above the editor."}

## Assembling the Reporting Package

A set of pages becomes a package when a reader can find their way through it and trust what it says. Navigation comes first. A page navigator is a group of buttons, one for each page, that Power BI keeps in step with the report: when you add, remove, rename, or reorder pages, the buttons follow (Microsoft, 2026b). Detail and tooltip pages are reached from the summary pages, so they are hidden from the page tabs and from the navigator. In Power BI Desktop, buttons respond to a click only while Ctrl is held, so that you can still select them to edit them; in the Power BI service they respond to a click.

A bookmark saves the current state of a page, such as its filters, its slicer selections, and which visuals are visible, so that a reader can return to it (Microsoft, 2025b). Bookmarks suit saved views, such as Furniture in fiscal 2026, or a version of a page prepared for a meeting. They are a poor way to build navigation, because a bookmark captures a page as it was, and every change to the page means updating it, while the page navigator updates itself. A field parameter lets a reader choose which measure or column a visual shows, from a slicer of field names, so that one chart can switch between, say, hours per standard hour and the overtime share. Power BI creates it as a small table that lists the fields with NAMEOF (Microsoft, 2026e). A field parameter cannot serve as the field of a drill-through or tooltip page, so those pages are linked to the underlying fields.

Documentation completes the package. Chapter 4 kept a Documentation worksheet in every workbook, and Chapter 13 promised its Power BI counterpart: an About page that states the purpose of the report, who it is for, where the data comes from and the period it covers, and what each KPI means, together with a description on every measure. The Validation page of Chapter 13 keeps reproducing the sales totals, and the Tests tab of Chapter 14 grows with each new page, so that the totals of the budget and the plant pages are tested against Chapters 7 and 11 the same way the sales totals were tested against Chapter 6.

::: {.callout-note .connecting-dots icon=false}
## Connecting the Dots
Every Part of this book has ended its tool's work with a way to make results repeatable and checkable: the Documentation worksheet and control totals of Chapter 4, the saved scripts and audit library of Part III, and now the About page, the measure descriptions, and the Tests tab. A report that managers act on every month is the strongest case for that discipline, because an error in it is repeated every month until someone finds it.
:::


{{< include _tutorial-03.qmd >}}


## What-If Parameters and Forecasts

Most of this chapter is descriptive and diagnostic analytics, in the terms of @tbl-01-01: it reports what happened and explains why. Power BI also supports the predictive and prescriptive questions of Chapter 7, with two features that need the same caution Chapter 7 applied in Excel.

A what-if parameter lets a reader change an assumption with a slider and watch the measures that use it change. Choosing Modeling > New parameter > Numeric range creates a one-column table of the values the slider allows and a measure that returns the value the reader selected, and can place the slider on the page (Microsoft, 2025d). A measure that refers to the parameter's value then recalculates with each move. The Part II case used Goal Seek to find the discount at which a promotion pays for itself: the increase in volume needed to earn the same margin after the discount, the break-even lift. With a what-if parameter for the discount, the same calculation becomes a page on which the sales manager can try discounts and see the lift each would require. The evidence the case examined, which found no lift, is what the reader must weigh the required lift against.

The Analytics pane of a line chart can add a forecast to a series of dates, with a chosen length and confidence interval (Microsoft, 2025e). The forecast uses exponential smoothing, a family of methods that weight recent observations more heavily than older ones and that can detect a seasonal pattern on their own, and it can also be run on older data to see how it would have predicted the recent past, a hindcast (Microsoft, 2014). Chapter 7's advice applies unchanged: a forecast is judged by how well it would have predicted periods you already know, against simple benchmarks such as the same period last year.

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
A forecast learns from whatever history the chart gives it. Charles River's three years of monthly revenue begin with a start-up month at about half the usual level, and its expense months with three pay dates come in a pattern that a seasonal model may or may not detect from three years of data. Before you show a forecast to a manager, fit it on data that ends before a quarter you know, compare it with that quarter's actual results and with Chapter 7's benchmarks, and say on the page how it was tested.
:::


## Looking Ahead

This chapter has turned the model of Chapter 14 into a reporting package for three readers. You designed pages around their questions, with each KPI shown against its comparison, and gave readers ways to reach the detail behind a number through drill-through pages and tooltips. You placed the budget beside the ledger and found that the largest variances of fiscal 2026 were volume and classification, not spending, and that what remained was a rate and a timing pattern the earlier chapters had already traced. You wrote visual calculations, saw where they stop being reliable, and kept the numbers readers depend on in measures with tests. The package now has navigation and an About page, and its Validation page and Tests tab tie every page to the earlier Parts. Most of this work was descriptive and diagnostic analytics; the what-if parameter and the forecast are its first predictive and prescriptive tools, each to be judged before it is trusted.

The package is ready for its readers, but not yet for its auditors. Chapter 16 turns to the internal auditor of Chapters 8 and 12, who will monitor the same data for exceptions, keep a record of what each exception turned out to be, and test whether the package itself can be relied on. How the package reaches its readers, and how each department manager sees only the cost center they manage, is the subject of [the appendix on publishing and security](#sec-appendix-publishing).
